newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Major says Kashmir solution would boost stability.
newsitem.headline: Major says Kashmir solution would boost stability.

text.p: LAHORE, Pakistan, Jan 14 (Pakistan) - British Prime Minister John Major on Tuesday called for talks to settle the Kashmir dispute bedevilling relations between Pakistan and India.
Major told reporters at the end of a week-long South Asian tour that Pakistan, India and the people of Kashmir all had an important part to play in deciding if a solution was possible.
"Self-evidently, one wants to ensure that comprehensive talks take place," he said in the Pakistani city of Lahore.
"I hope the governments will be able to get together. I hope they will be able to take full account of the people who actually live in Kashmir."
A Moslem separatist revolt against Indian rule in the two-thirds of Kashmir under New Delhi's control has cost an estimated 20,000 lives since 1990.

Pakistan, which holds the remaining third of the disputed Himalayan region, denies Indian charges that it has been arming, training and financing the Kashmiri militants, who are fighting for independence or union with Islamic Pakistan.
Major said Britain would be "happy to lend a hand" if outside assistance was asked for and thought appropriate.

"But essentially an agreement will have to be reached in this part of the world. It cannot be imposed," he said. "It undoubtedly will require skill, wisdom and courage by both (Indian and Pakistani) governments...
"If it were to be solved in the next few years, I think it will be a key to unlocking greater stability, investment and prosperity in years to come," Major said.
The British prime minister said the main focus of his trip had been to promote trade with Pakistan and British investment, which has grown almost four-fold in the past three years.
Driving home his message that Pakistan must not jettison democracy, he said: "Trade and investment will only flourish in the long term against a stable political background."
The final day of Major's tour was packed with visits to British aid schemes, a joint venture project and a seminar given by British businessmen in the Punjab provincial capital, Lahore.
Major, who has steered a careful course through the turbulent political scene during his two days in Pakistan, praised the "tremendous untapped potential" of the country.
Major has held talks with top political figures, including caretaker prime minister Meraj Khalid, Benazir Bhutto, whom Khalid replaced, Nawaz Sharif and President Farooq Leghari.

He has stressed that he looks forward to elections due next month to a new National Assembly to replace the one dissolved by Leghari after he dismissed Bhutto as prime minister on disputed charges of corruption and misrule on November 5.

The Lahore visit follows a whistle-stop tour on Monday to the top of the Khyber Pass, the route taken by invaders from Darius of Persia to Alexander the Great's generals and warring Afghan tribes, and now the route for most of Europe's heroin.
Major told troops from Pakistan's crack Frontier Corps that Britain would consider making up shortfalls in the equipment they use to try to halt the flow of drugs.
Major was enthusiastically cheered by crowds of brightly clad Pakistani schoolchilden as he arrived in Lahore.
He was mobbed in India by businessmen and women, and praised by Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina for his efforts to boost trade.

But the warm glow of Major's welcome is unlikely to last long on his return to Britain on Tuesday night -- he faces an election just four months away and he is some 20 points behind in the opinion polls.
